summary: The 7-bit code that gave every letter, digit and control key a number. It let computers from different makers exchange text and survives as the first 128 characters of Unicode.

events.note: Work starts after IBM engineer Bob Bemer proposes a common code.
The first edition is published as ASA X3.4-1963.

events.label: Revision
events.note: A major revision adds lower-case letters in their final places.

events.label: Federal rule
events.note: President Johnson requires US government computers to support it.

events.label: Last update
events.note: ANSI X3.4-1986, the last major update.

events.label: UTF-8 wins
events.note: UTF-8 overtakes ASCII as the most common encoding on the Web.
